overview: The map’s Zhou states label groups rival polities across 500 to 200 BCE. It does not show a single united kingdom. Much of this interval belongs to the Warring States era, when rulers, craftspeople and thinkers reshaped society. The outline continues beyond Qin’s unification in 221 BCE and therefore cannot represent independent Zhou-era states throughout.

periods.title: Late Spring and Autumn
periods.summary: The imported record begins before the conventional Warring States boundary.

periods.title: Warring States rivalry
periods.summary: Powerful kingdoms competed while the Zhou royal dynasty persisted with diminished authority.

periods.title: After the Zhou kings
periods.summary: Rival kingdoms survived the royal dynasty until Qin defeated its competitors.

periods.title: Beyond the old state system
periods.summary: The final mapped years belong to Qin and early Han imperial history.

items.text: In fourth-century BCE Qin, the reformer Shang Yang sought to concentrate resources on farming and warfare. Written rules promised rewards and threatened punishments. The Book of Lord Shang preserves a harsh political vision: producing grain and fighting for the state mattered more to its authors than cultivating a comfortable private life.

Thinkers offered different answers to the problem of disorder. Confucian traditions emphasized moral conduct and family relationships; Daoist approaches looked to the patterns of nature; Legalist arguments favored strong government and systematic rewards and punishments. These debates outlived the kingdoms in which they developed.

Money reveals regional variety. The British Museum displays knife-shaped currency from northern states and round coins with holes from Wei, Qi and Yan. Knife money retained a ring and ridges resembling a tool. A coin did not have to be a round disk.

At Matengkong in the Guanzhong basin, researchers floated soil from pits, house floors and kilns to recover charred seeds. The samples span the Warring States and Qin imperial periods. Foxtail millet and wheat dominated the crop remains, with beans and other crops also present: evidence of varied farming rather than a rice-only diet.

The Matengkong study counted more than 15,000 foxtail millet grains but only ten rice grains. That does not mean a household ate exactly those proportions. Preservation, grain size and how food was discarded affect what survives. The researchers found no supporting evidence that rice was grown locally at this particular site.

A bronze cooler from Marquis Yi of Zeng’s tomb held a smaller wine vessel inside a larger container, with ice packed between their walls. Hooks secured the inner vessel, and a ladle was recovered with it. This was an elite feast’s carefully engineered cooler, without an electric plug in sight.

A painted pottery food vessel at the Met, dated to the fifth or fourth century BCE, was made for burial as a substitute for bronze or lacquer tableware. Similar examples came from Zhongshan tombs. Such objects show how people equipped the dead, rather than proving that this particular dish served someone’s dinner.

An elite owner’s bronze mirror, now at the University of Michigan, had a smooth, polished face and a back covered with curling, dragon-like patterns. The shiny metal supplied the reflection. Its patterned back was decorative: the ancient equivalent of caring what both sides of a personal accessory looked like.

Lacquer could do more than decorate a cup. Hubei Provincial Museum explains that Warring States shields could be built by applying many layers over a leather base. Once dry, the coating made a hard surface for painted patterns. The same broad craft tradition served both ceremonial display and protection in fighting.

Marquis Yi’s tomb near present-day Suizhou offers an unusually rich glimpse of a court. A gift bell from the ruler of Chu bears a date corresponding to 433 BCE, helping date the burial. Musical instruments, ritual vessels and manuscripts survived together, linking diplomatic gifts with the marquis’s own ceremonial world.

Some ancient bronze bells can produce two different notes. Their cross-section resembles a lens rather than a circle: strike near the center of a face for one tone, or toward the side for another. Smithsonian acoustic research explains the different vibration patterns. One bell could effectively do two musical jobs.

A duck-shaped lacquer case from an accompanying coffin in Marquis Yi’s tomb carries pictures of dancing, bells and drums. The museum suggests it belonged to a woman buried there. A practical container thus preserves images of performance; it also reminds us that the tomb contained people besides its famous ruler.

A wooden chest from the same tomb carried a sky diagram on its lid: the Big Dipper at the center, twenty-eight named star groupings around it, and a dragon and tiger at the sides. Astronomy could appear on a portable possession. This is a specific elite object, not evidence that every child owned a star chart.

A lacquered wooden deer from Marquis Yi’s tomb has real antlers and a head that can turn. Holes in its legs and its position among instruments led the museum to suggest it supported a drum. That interpretation is not certain, but the moving head shows how lively a crafted object could be.

sections.title: Learning, writing and worries about illness

items.text: Tomb M798 at Wangjiazui in Chu, dated to around 300 BCE, contained approximately 800 bamboo strips alongside bronze and lacquer objects. One group records sayings attributed to Confucius. Researchers identify more than one scribe’s handwriting, showing that making a text could involve several writers rather than a single author at a desk.

A short written sample from that Wangjiazui collection is 孔子曰, read in modern Mandarin as Kongzi yue: “Confucius said.” These are scholars’ standard modern Chinese characters for an attested ancient formula, not a reproduction of the bamboo handwriting. It introduces sayings attributed to the teacher; it is not evidence that Confucius personally wrote the surviving strips.

The Guodian manuscripts, buried in Chu around 300 BCE, do not all agree with one another. Historian Andrew Meyer argues that some may have been collected as useful arguments against intellectual opponents. Imagine a collection for debating difficult questions, rather than a textbook whose every page gives the same answer.

Bamboo records from Baoshan tomb 2 preserve official Shao Tuo’s worries between 318 and 316 BCE. Diviners asked about his service to the king and, increasingly, his illness. The records describe abdominal trouble and difficulty eating. These are unusually personal glimpses of suffering, but they do not establish a secure modern diagnosis.

Shao Tuo consulted several diviners using tortoise and yarrow methods, and their conclusions could differ. They proposed sacrifices and rites to address perceived causes of his illness. The records even preserve hopeful predictions before his death. We can study what these people believed without treating their predictions as effective medical treatment.

ending.text: The Zhou royal dynasty ended in 256 BCE, but the competing kingdoms did not all end with it. Qin’s victories culminated in unification in 221 BCE. Their independent governments disappeared, while people, crafts and intellectual traditions continued under imperial rule. The map’s extension to 200 BCE is not a later survival of the Warring States.
